subject: chemistry_2
question_text: What type of bonding helps in stabilizing the α-helix structure of proteins?

verification.note: Unit 13 (Biomolecules) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 10 "BIOMOLECULES", book pp.99-104; the book prints this question on book p.99 as VSAQ 10. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The type of bond
lines: The bonding is intramolecular: both groups
belong to the same polypeptide chain.
The hydrogen bonds are weak on their own,
but there are many of them along the coil.
steps.why: Hydrogen bonding is what holds the coil; the peptide bonds hold the chain itself and are not what the question asks about. Calling it intramolecular is the word that separates the helix from the β-sheet, where the bonds run between separate chains.
common_mistakes: Answering "peptide bond". The peptide bond joins the amino acids; hydrogen bonds hold the coil.
Calling the bonding intermolecular. In the α-helix both groups are on the same chain.
steps.memory_tip: Peptide bonds make the chain; hydrogen bonds make the coil.
steps.margin_note: The word "hydrogen bonding" alone is worth about half. Add "intramolecular" to secure the mark.

steps.label: The groups joined

lines.text: N–H of one residue to O=C of another

lines: The bond forms between the –NH group of one
amino acid residue and the >C=O group of a
residue in the adjacent turn of the helix.
Every turn is held this way, so the coil
keeps its shape along its whole length.
steps.why: Naming the two groups is what turns "hydrogen bonding" into an answer. The >C=O and –NH groups both belong to the peptide backbone, not to the side chains, which is why every protein can form a helix whatever its side chains are.
common_mistakes: Writing that the side chains, the R groups, form the hydrogen bonds. The bonds are between the backbone –NH and >C=O groups.
Saying the bond joins two –NH groups. It joins an –NH group to a >C=O group.
steps.memory_tip: N–H gives the hydrogen; O of C=O receives it, one turn away.
steps.margin_note: Name both groups, –NH and >C=O, and say they are in adjacent turns. That is the second mark.

insider_note: The answer is two words and two groups: hydrogen bonding, between the –NH and the >C=O of the same chain. Do not write "peptide bond"; that is the commonest wrong answer here.
